title: Princess Sophia, suffragette
hookLine: Duleep's daughter Sophia campaigned for women's votes in Britain

cards: Outside the gates of Hampton Court Palace, near London, a woman in a fine coat holds up a newspaper for sale. It's called The Suffragette. People walking past might know her face.

She lives just across the road, in a grace-and-favor house the old Queen herself granted her. She is a goddaughter of Queen Victoria. Her father was the last Maharaja of the Sikh kingdom, the boy who lost a crown.
And here she is on the pavement, selling a paper that demands the vote for women.

teach.h: A COMFORTABLE LIFE AT HAMPTON COURT.
teach.b: Sophia Duleep Singh grew up English in every outward way: country houses, ponies, dresses, and later a grace-and-favor home at Hampton Court. She could have stayed there quietly, and nobody would have blinked.

teach.h: A JOURNEY TO INDIA CHANGED HER.
teach.b: As her biographer Anita Anand tells it, a journey to India changed her. She saw Punjab, the land her father had ruled, and people living under a government they had no voice in.
Back in Britain, women had no vote either. She joined the women fighting for one, the suffragettes, and she didn't do it from the back row.
She walked with the women who went to Parliament to demand the vote, on a day when the crowd was met with force. She refused to pay her taxes, saying in effect: no vote, no tax.
So officials seized her things, jewelry among them, and sold them at auction, and the fight went on.
Guru Nanak, in the Asa di Var, asks why anyone would speak ill of woman, when it is from woman that kings themselves are born.
Sophia was raised far from the Gurus' hymns, and nobody can say how much of them she knew.
But a daughter of the Sikh royal house stood in the street for women's equal voice, and the old line and the new march sound alike.

how: Sikhs in Britain remember Princess Sophia Duleep Singh as a suffragette, and her story is often told alongside the Gurus' teaching that women and men are equal in the sangat.

games.q: you're Sophia. the tax bill comes, and women still have no vote. you can afford to pay. what do you do?
o: pay it quietly and keep your peace.
refuse to pay: no vote, no tax.
games.why: she refused. officials seized her things, jewelry among them, and auctioned them, and she kept campaigning.

practice: Bring to mind one cause you think is fair, large or small: a neighbor who isn't being heard, a rule at work that falls hard on some people, a question of who gets a say.
Don't argue it out; just hold it, and let one small, peaceful thing you could do for it come to mind, a signature, a phone call, a word in a meeting. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over it.
